name: FourQlib (SchnorrQ / FourQ curve arithmetic)
baseline: NIST P-256 (Gueron-Krasnov fast implementation, the code later merged into OpenSSL as nistz256)
workload: Variable-base and fixed-base elliptic-curve scalar multiplication (the core operation underlying ECDH and SchnorrQ signing/verification), modeled as one ephemeral Diffie-Hellman round, on several x64 CPUs
claimed_speedup: up to 5.6x faster than the NIST P-256 implementation in [Gueron-Krasnov] for variable-base scalar mult; up to 4.4x faster for a full ephemeral-DH round; 2.2-2.9x faster than Curve25519 implementations
hardware: Intel Atom N570 (1.66GHz), Core i7-2600 Sandy Bridge (3.4GHz), Core i7-3770 Ivy Bridge (3.4GHz), Core i7-4770 Haswell (3.4GHz), Core i5-5300U Broadwell (2.30GHz), AMD A8 PRO-7600B Kaveri (3.1GHz); TurboBoost/TurboCore disabled
tradeoffs: FourQ is a non-NIST, non-standardized curve, so adopting it trades interoperability/standard compliance for speed; correct use requires careful handling of the curve's cofactor and endomorphisms for security.
caveats: The numeric comparison in the ASIACRYPT 2015 paper (Table 5) is against the standalone Gueron-Krasnov P-256 implementation, not literally the OpenSSL library, and predates OpenSSL's own nistz256 merge; compiler/flags for the comparison are not stated (CPU models are), so tier is capped at B; benchmarks are from 2012-2015-era CPUs; no separate cycle-count benchmark specifically for SchnorrQ signing/verification (as opposed to raw scalar multiplication) was found in the FourQ or SchnorrQ papers.
found_via: Query: 'FourQlib' / 'FourQ SchnorrQ eBACS' on GitHub search; opened microsoft/FourQlib repo, then the FourQ ASIACRYPT 2015 paper (eprint 2015/565) and the SchnorrQ MSR tech report for the underlying claim

name: Ed25519 (original amd64-64-24k SUPERCOP/eBATS submission)
baseline: OpenSSL ECDSA (NIST P-256), benchmarked as SUPERCOP/eBATS entry 'ecdonaldp256' (an OpenSSL-based ECDSA wrapper)
workload: Single-signature signing and verification (and batch verification of 64 signatures) on an Intel Xeon E5620 Westmere core (machine 'hydra2'), measured in CPU cycles via the eBATS benchmarking framework
claimed_speedup: Signing: 87548 cycles vs OpenSSL ECDSA's 1790936 cycles (~20.5x faster). Single-signature verification: 273364 cycles vs OpenSSL ECDSA's 2087500 cycles (~7.6x faster); batch verification (64 sigs): ~134000 cycles/sig (~15.6x faster)
hardware: Intel Xeon E5620 (Westmere), machine 'hydra2', Turbo Boost disabled
stars_or_usage: Foundational EdDSA implementation; later adopted (with modifications) by libsodium, OpenSSH, OpenSSL 1.1+, GnuPG, Signal, and most modern TLS stacks
tradeoffs: Ed25519 uses a fixed, non-NIST curve and deterministic nonces, which differ from ECDSA's API/semantics and key format; this original submission is unpadded raw assembly (amd64-64-24k), not a general-purpose library API.
caveats: Compiler and optimization flags for the benchmark are not stated in the paper itself (only in the underlying eBATS machine-readable data, which was not independently opened this session), so tier capped at B; the OpenSSL comparison figure ('ecdonaldp256') is an eBATS-submitted OpenSSL wrapper rather than a raw 'openssl speed' run, though it is described in the paper as using OpenSSL's ECDSA/NIST P-256 code; add 'no patent grant' caveat per public-domain dedication.
found_via: Starting query 'SUPERCOP eBATS signature KEM benchmark fastest implementations' -> bench.cr.yp.to results-sign.html -> Bernstein/Duif/Lange/Schwabe/Yang 'High-speed high-security signatures' (JCEN 2012) paper

name: Optimizing Dilithium Implementation with AVX2/AVX-512 (PSPM)
baseline: liboqs / PQClean Dilithium AVX2 implementation (and the pq-crystals/dilithium reference AVX2 code that liboqs wraps)
workload: ML-DSA/Dilithium2, Dilithium3, and Dilithium5 key generation, signing, and verification, using a new 'PSPM' (parallel small-polynomial multiplication) technique instead of NTT for the AVX-512 path
claimed_speedup: AVX-512 vs AVX2: keygen +43.2%/39.3%/45.6%, signing +36.6%/41.6%/43.7%, verification +45.3%/46.5%/47.4% for Dilithium2/3/5 respectively; PSPM itself is 47-66% faster than NTT-based small-polynomial multiplication in the AVX2/AVX-512 comparison
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 hardware support (not present on all deployed x86-64 CPUs, and historically disabled on some consumer Intel chips); the PSPM technique changes the internal multiplication algorithm, so it is not a drop-in replacement without re-verifying constant-time behavior.
caveats: No license file in the repo (base code derives from the public-domain/CC0-ish NIST reference Dilithium and MIT-licensed PQClean, but the author's own PSPM code carries no explicit license) -> usability marked 'mixed'; the paper's own abstract states 'we will later open source our code', and this repo (by an author matching the paper's optimization, PSPM) appears to be that release, though it is not explicitly linked from the arXiv paper itself.
found_via: arXiv search 'Dilithium faster' -> arXiv:2306.01989 'Optimized Vectorization Implementation of CRYSTALS-Dilithium' -> GitHub code search for 'PSPM dilithium' locating the matching source repo

name: ML-KEM AVX-512 optimization for TLS 1.3 (Zheng et al., Fudan University)
workload: ML-KEM-512/768/1024 key generation, encapsulation, and decapsulation, plus a batch key-generation variant, integrated into liboqs and OQS-provider for OpenSSL/TLS 1.3 handshakes
claimed_speedup: Up to 1.64x speedup over the latest AVX2 implementation for core ML-KEM operations; batch key generation is 3.5x-4.9x faster; results in more TLS 1.3 handshakes/sec in both PQ-only and hybrid modes
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8475B, 4 vCPUs, 8 GiB memory (Alibaba Cloud c8i compute-optimized instance, Sapphire Rapids)
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512; the paper's batch key-generation method requires protocol-level changes to how TLS 1.3 handshakes request/consume KEM keys, not just a drop-in library swap.
caveats: Paper explicitly states 'we will later open source our code' and no matching public repository could be found this session, so has_code=false and tier capped at C despite compiler/CPU/OpenSSL-version being stated; peer-review venue for this arXiv preprint is unconfirmed.
found_via: arXiv search 'ML-KEM AVX' -> arXiv:2404.13544 'Faster Post-Quantum TLS 1.3 Based on ML-KEM: Implementation and Assessment'

name: libsecp256k1
workload: secp256k1 ECDSA signing, verification, and key generation, as used in Bitcoin Core transaction validation
claimed_speedup: Not quantified with numbers in the primary sources checked this session; Bitcoin Core's v0.10.0 release notes and contemporaneous commentary describe libsecp256k1 as faster than (and more side-channel-resistant than) OpenSSL's generic ECDSA/secp256k1 code, which motivated Bitcoin Core's 2015 switch away from OpenSSL for signing and (later) verification
stars_or_usage: 2.5k stars; the ECDSA/Schnorr library used by Bitcoin Core, and widely reused elsewhere (Ethereum, other cryptocurrencies)
tradeoffs: Curve-specific (secp256k1 only), so not a general-purpose EC library replacement for OpenSSL; API surface is intentionally narrow.
caveats: Could not locate a primary source with an explicit numeric speedup figure in the time available (Bitcoin Core release notes, the project README, and a Bitcoin wiki page were checked and only describe qualitative performance/security advantages); only 1 tier-D entry included per the assignment's cap, chosen here because the project is highly notable and the 'faster than OpenSSL' claim is well-documented qualitatively.
found_via: GitHub search 'faster than OpenSSL ecdsa' variants and direct lookup of bitcoin-core/secp256k1; HN Algolia query 'libsecp256k1 openssl' surfacing the r/Bitcoin discussion of the 0.10.0 release notes
